heading: Introduction
subtitle: Five labels capture different forms of group-related language
speaker: Introduce StereoDetect as a benchmark-based project. The dataset and definitions are prior work; this project compares model families, task adaptation, structured output, and diagnostic explanations.

heading: Literature Review
subtitle: Dataset foundations and explainable stereotype detection
speaker: StereoDetect supplies the five-class task and benchmark definitions. HEARTS supplies a related ALBERT-based binary stereotype detection and explainability approach. Its task and dataset differ from this project; its published scores are not mixed into the local comparison.

heading: Literature Review
subtitle: Model families used in the comparison
speaker: This slide describes public model backbones. The exact classifier fitting details for the MiniLM and Qwen3-Embedding baseline runs are not present in the supplied code; their scores are reported from DL-Review-2.docx. Later diagrams mark those task heads as schematic.

heading: Motivation
subtitle: Test both classification quality and the usefulness of the output
speaker: Frame these as project questions, not as claims that no earlier work exists. Dataset-specific label meanings make task adaptation worth measuring. The richer-input label task and sentence-only JSON task must be interpreted separately.

heading: Problem Statement
subtitle: Three Qwen task contracts on the same held-out test split
speaker: There are three independent task adapters: sentence-only numeric labels, metadata-conditioned numeric labels, and sentence-only category/target/label JSON. Each is compared to the base checkpoint under its own prompt. All report the same held-out 1,738 rows. Metadata-conditioned results should not be read as input-matched rankings against sentence-only models.

heading: Architecture
subtitle: Overall experimental pipeline
speaker: The dataset is split before model training. Validation selects checkpoints; held-out test evaluation reports task-specific scores. Explanations are produced for saved ALBERT and ModernBERT-large classifiers. Public-backbone baseline scores are retained from the review document.

heading: Architecture
subtitle: all-MiniLM-L6-v2 · Compact sentence-embedding backbone
speaker: The published all-MiniLM-L6-v2 backbone uses six transformer layers, 384-dimensional hidden states, mean pooling, and normalized sentence embeddings. The dashed task stage is schematic: the supplied review records its five-class score, but does not include the downstream classifier implementation. Do not imply that a particular classifier or training recipe was verified.

heading: Architecture
subtitle: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B · Decoder-derived sentence representation
speaker: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B uses a dense Qwen3 decoder backbone with 28 layers. Its official model extracts a final-token representation and supports an embedding dimension up to 1,024. The supplied materials report a five-class baseline score but omit the downstream classifier details, so that stage is explicitly schematic.

heading: Architecture
subtitle: ALBERT-base-v2 · Sentence-only five-class classifier
speaker: ALBERT factorizes token embeddings and shares parameters across repeated transformer layers. The local classifier consumes Sentence only, applies the ALBERT pooler to the classification token, and produces five label logits. Category and Target are metadata, not model inputs. This differs from the wording in one row of the supplied review document; the diagram follows the actual code and run configuration.

heading: Architecture
subtitle: ModernBERT-large · Sentence-only five-class classifier
speaker: This architecture slide describes the saved large-model run; additional base-model experiments are reported in the appendix. The saved configuration has 28 encoder layers, hidden width 1,024, local attention width 128, and global attention every third layer. The classification pooler is mean pooling in the saved configuration; it is not a CLS-only head. RoPE and GeGLU are public backbone design features. The training settings shown are for the additional saved large-model run, rather than an inferred recipe for the earlier review score.

heading: Architecture
subtitle: Qwen3.5-2B · Shared language backbone, three task adapters
speaker: This project uses only the language path of the conditional-generation model. The official 2B text configuration contains 24 layers arranged in six repetitions of three linear-attention layers followed by one full-attention layer. Gated DeltaNet is used for the linear-attention path. LoRA is trained separately for sentence-only labels, conditioned labels, and JSON; the three adapters are not interchangeable. Rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05 are taken from the implementation. No vision input is used.

heading: Architecture
subtitle: Aligned word-level explanations for the encoder classifiers
speaker: Both explainers treat each word occurrence as a feature and replace absent words with the tokenizer mask token. LIME uses 1,000 perturbations. Kernel SHAP uses an all-masked baseline and up to 512 coalitions with no L1 feature selection. Predictions are made on the same perturbed strings by the saved encoder classifier. Explanations concern class probabilities, not moral judgments about words or calibrated prediction confidence. The 100-example sample is deliberately diagnostic and not representative test statistics.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: Dataset, training setup, and evaluation protocol
speaker: The new sentence-only Qwen LoRA uses two T4 GPUs, batch 16 per GPU, global batch 32, three epochs and 570 optimizer steps. It trains in FP32 with LoRA rank 16, alpha 32 and dropout 0.05. The matching base evaluation uses vLLM BF16 on H100 MIG 0. Prompt, test rows and five-label argmax scoring match, but numerical precision and runtime differ. Validation macro F1 selected epoch 3; test was evaluated once after loading that adapter. Other Qwen adapters retain effective batch 16.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: Model comparison on the 1,738-example test split
speaker: The new sentence-only Qwen label result is 93.84% accuracy and 93.89% macro F1. The conditioned label adapter is a different experiment and receives gold category and target as input. Review-only baseline rows are preserved rather than replaced by later saved runs. Additional saved ModernBERT-base experiments and all full classification reports are included in the appendix. Precision/runtime differ across experiments, so this is descriptive rather than an engine-controlled model ranking.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: Qwen3.5-2B · Three tasks × Base / SFT
speaker: Exactly six canonical full-test evaluations: three tasks, each with base and task-specific supervised fine-tuning via LoRA. Base is the same pretrained checkpoint under three prompts. Each SFT task uses its own adapter. Task B predicts category, target and label jointly; the summary scores only its label field. C receives gold category and target as input. We select the standalone test evaluations for B and C, and the completed Kaggle test evaluation for A. Earlier training-time test passes are repeated evaluations, not extra models. All runs disable thinking and use the same 1,738 test rows. Numerical engines and precision differ.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: A · Sentence → label · Base vs SFT
speaker: Both runs take only Sentence and select the largest logit among label tokens 0-4 with thinking disabled. Base has 403 correct, LoRA 1,631 correct out of 1,738. Accuracy rises from 23.19% to 93.84%, an observed gain of 70.66 percentage points. Macro F1 rises from 14.21% to 93.89%. Base uses vLLM BF16; the adapter uses PyTorch FP32, so this is not a precision/engine-controlled ablation.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: B · Sentence → category + target + label · Base vs SFT
speaker: Both runs receive only Sentence and generate category, target and label JSON. This chart scores the label field only; it does not mean all fields are correct. Greedy generation and a 96-token cap are used in the saved task configuration. The base run has 599 correct labels, the adapter run 1,627. Both saved evaluations record zero invalid labels. The distinct complete-JSON result appears on the next slide.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: B · Generated JSON · Per-field and all-fields accuracy
speaker: Every saved completion is aligned with its source test row. Category is compared after trimming, case folding and collapsing whitespace. Target uses exact string comparison, including capitalization and underscores. Label must be an integer matching the gold label. Complete JSON accuracy requires all three fields to be correct for the same example. Both sets contain valid JSON objects for all 1,738 rows, so low base accuracy is semantic rather than just JSON formatting. The fine-tuned all-field count agrees with the existing field_validation.json. Base field metrics were computed from saved completions while preparing this deck; no model was rerun.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: B · Generated JSON · Per-field accuracy and macro F1
speaker: This supplements the exact-match field accuracy slide with full classification macro F1. Categories use five fixed normalized classes. Targets use the 87 exact gold target strings, preserving case and underscores. Predictions outside the gold class set are incorrect and appear in the companion reports; macro averages are over the explicit gold class set. The training-time and standalone JSON adapter evaluations have identical category and target prediction vectors and differ on one label. This table uses the standalone adapter evaluation.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: C · Sentence + category + target → label · Base vs SFT
speaker: Both runs use Category, Target and Sentence, and choose among the five numeric label-token logits. The base benchmark evaluates the Qwen/Qwen3.5-2B checkpoint without a task adapter; the fine-tuned run loads outputs/qwen35_2b_stereodetect/adapter. Accuracy gain is computed in percentage points, not relative percent. Engines differ (vLLM versus Transformers/PEFT), so this is an observed task-adaptation comparison rather than an isolated engine-controlled ablation.

heading: Experimental Results
subtitle: Stereotype versus anti-stereotype remains the hardest boundary
speaker: Across these three sentence-only experiments, classes 0 and 1 have lower F1 than the neutral and bias classes. For the new sentence-only Qwen LoRA, 46 anti-stereotypes become stereotypes and 36 stereotypes become anti-stereotypes: 82 of 107 errors. This is a confusion-matrix observation, not a linguistic causal explanation.

heading: Demonstration
subtitle: Saved test example · Same sentence, different structured predictions
speaker: This demonstration replays saved responses for test index 0 and is not a fresh model inference. Dataset annotation: Category Neutral, Target Neutral, Label 2. The base model instead targets dog and predicts class 3. The task adapter recovers the annotated neutral target and class 2. This is a single illustration rather than an estimate of overall accuracy.

heading: Demonstration
subtitle: ModernBERT-large · Correct prediction with word color maps
speaker: Saved diagnostic test index 1713. Exact word occurrences and attribution arrays are reused; no new explanation inference was run. Gold label 1; model label 1. Both rows explain the predicted class 1. Blue denotes a negative contribution/weight for this class; orange denotes positive; near-white is close to zero. Both slides share a fixed symmetric scale -0.70 to +0.70. LIME surrogate weights and Kernel SHAP contributions are distinct quantities and not word probabilities. Attributions diagnose model sensitivity and do not certify correctness. Signed values are displayed to three decimals.

speaker: Saved diagnostic test index 1205. Exact word occurrences and attribution arrays are reused; no new explanation inference was run. Gold label 4; model label 0. heading: Conclusion
subtitle: Task adaptation improves all three task setups
speaker: The new sentence-only label experiment improves from 23.19% to 93.84% accuracy under matched prompt, split and label-token scoring, with differing precision/runtime. The metadata-conditioned label adapter reaches 95.51%; its richer inputs prevent a direct input-matched ranking. Sentence-only JSON label accuracy is 93.61%, category accuracy 99.37%, target exact match 98.16%, and all-three-fields accuracy 92.87%. The explanation examples use ModernBERT-large, not Qwen, and include a misclassification to show why attribution does not certify correctness. Future work is proposed, not performed.
